content: The effective coordination of testing services at the national level is crucial for establishing a sustainable and efficient national hepatitis testing program. Key elements for countries to consider when planning or expanding viral hepatitis testing include ensuring the quality and accuracy of testing services. A national technical working group should be established to address various laboratory aspects. This group should include representatives from patient groups, civil society, public and private testing providers, government agencies, laboratory specialists, program experts, and other stakeholders. A national hepatitis testing policy should outline the goals and objectives of testing services, define responsibilities at each level of the testing network, and align with broader health policies. This policy should also address the needs of at-risk populations, such as those in prisons or closed settings, and engage stakeholders to build consensus on national testing priorities. It should contribute to the development of a strategic plan for hepatitis testing, encompassing diagnosis, prevention, surveillance, and treatment. Strategic planning for testing services requires a situation analysis to map existing facilities capable of conducting hepatitis testing, assess their infrastructure, technical and human resources, and financing. A minimum package of testing services should be defined for each level of the healthcare system, with appropriate budgets and infrastructure in place. National regulatory mechanisms must oversee the quality and safety of diagnostics, staff, and services. This includes pre-market and post-market controls for in vitro diagnostics (IVDs), certification of testing staff, and accreditation of testing services. For countries lacking regulatory capacity, the WHO prequalification assessment can provide independent evaluations of IVD quality, safety, and performance. A national reference laboratory should be designated to oversee quality control, organize quality assessment schemes, and provide training and supervisory support. Building capacity for hepatitis testing services should be integrated into broader efforts to expand access to testing for related diseases, such as HIV, and address co-infections like HIV/HCV. This requires a trained and motivated workforce across disease control programs. Human resource management is critical, with personnel such as phlebotomists, laboratory technicians, and data clerks requiring appropriate training, certification, and supervision. Testing facilities must be well-designed and maintained, with clean, safe environments for specimen collection and testing. Universal precautions should be followed to prevent occupational hazards, and proper waste disposal systems must be in place. Testing should ideally occur in climate-controlled areas to maintain assay performance. Testing services should be organized across different levels of the healthcare system, with rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) enabling broader access at primary care levels. Specimen integrity is critical for accurate testing, and proper collection, storage, and processing methods must be followed as per manufacturer instructions. Venous whole blood, plasma, and dried blood spots (DBS) are commonly used specimens, with specific requirements for handling and storage. Pre-test and post-test counseling are essential components of hepatitis testing services. Counseling should address the five Cs: consent, confidentiality, counseling, correct test results, and connection to care.
